Privileged access is still very common in crypto.

We talk a lot about decentralization, but less about who gets to see sensitive information before a decision is made.

Let's take sealed-bid auctions as an example, where the bidders can't see each other's bids.

It might sound private enough at first, but someone still has to resolve the auction, which means one party gets access to every bid.

I really hadn’t really thought about this trust assumption until I stumbled upon @theInterfold’s latest blog piece (recommend giving it a read).

Their setup tackles that privileged-access problem directly. Bids stay private, while the final result can still be verified without one operator seeing everything.

It's definitely a better-suited model for token sales, solver markets, and blockspace auctions.

Disclosure: Big supporter of Interfold's confidential coordination vision.

Confidential markets are about more than hiding transactions.

I use prediction markets a lot around major events.

Especially @Polymarket, as it's objectively the most liquid venue for most people to trade these events.

With the recent addition of Perps, there's a lot more flexibility around the same events.

Basically, it gives me more ways to trade & hedge the same event without forcing every view into a YES/NO market and increases my exposure through leverage.

Let's take tomorrow's Fed decision, for example: if I think the Fed will cut rates, I can:

→ Trade that outcome directly by buying YES shares in that market
→ Long or short BTC depending on how I think the market reacts

Either way, it's a pretty useful combination to have on one platform.

Batching, gasless and delegation (moreso than automation) are obvious use cases going back longer than that. It’s why we had a startup centered around it in 2020. 

A very complicated upgrade to consensus isn’t worth that though. There are simpler ways to do that. Especially for gasless and batching which are possible today. (In fact, delegation is also possible today?). The issue is lack of HW support. 

Delegation has an extra problem of verifying what rights you are granted to others (have you tried using a vault product like KPK and checking the zodiac module permissions? The UX is awful). 

Auth, I think is controversial. Not only because HW etc needs to implement it, but implementing verification algorithms for cryptographic protocols in Solidity is slow and error prone. That’s why BTCers have spent years on a super fast ecdsa / schnorr implementation.

Aka this is why I think 8130 is a mistake at consensus. It doesnt matter if a solution ticks all the boxes if it is crazy complicated and over engineered. That technical debt on nodes will be painful and probably lead to loss of user funds.
